article.title: Under the weather
article.description: Meaning: feeling slightly ill. Example: 'I'm feeling a bit under the weather today, I might stay home.' Register: informal, commonly used with close colleagues or friends rather than in very formal writing.
article.content: Meaning: feeling slightly ill. Example: 'I'm feeling a bit under the weather today, I might stay home.' Register: informal, commonly used with close colleagues or friends rather than in very formal writing.

generated.caption:
Ever felt a little unwell but not quite sick enough for a full-blown explanation? 🤒 We have the perfect idiom for you: "under the weather."

This simply means you're feeling slightly ill. It's an informal phrase, commonly used when chatting with friends or close colleagues. For instance: "I'm feeling a bit under the weather today, I might stay home."

slides.headlineRest: — What it Means When You're Not Feeling Well
slides.body: Have you ever heard someone say they're 'under the weather'? This common English idiom means feeling slightly ill or unwell. For example, you might say, 'I'm feeling a bit under the weather today, I might stay home.' It's an informal phrase, best used when talking to friends or close colleagues, rather than in very formal writing. So, next time you're not feeling your best, you know just what to say!
